correctness.rationale: Six vertices for every t>1/2, nine exact two-facet adjoint norm expressions, and an algebraically checked sharp envelope reduce the supremum over all real vectors and all positive t to one 2x2 Rayleigh quotient. The eigenvector lies in the required cone; explicit primal vertex pairs realize equality on both sides of t=1. The square case, monotone profile, and all claimed boundary derivatives follow. Standalone supplementary diagnostic 5777 checks corroborates but is not used as a continuum proof.

In the present transformed family ψ=ψ_{0,β} with β=1/(2−a), a=1/(2t) in (0,1); ψ(z)=max(1−(1−a)z,z) > ψ2(z) for sufficiently small z>0, so their Theorem 3.2 is inapplicable.
broader_coverage.reasoning: General theorems about C_NJ and uniform non-squareness, and fixed-regular-hexagon evaluations, do not imply the nonregular family law. The 2016 Day–James comparison is plausible but its abstract specifies a different p-family, and its full text was not obtained; this remains a named residual priority risk rather than a falsely certified negative. Important full-text comparison: Komuro–Saito–Mitani (2010) does classify this family among extreme absolute norms after the invertible change (s,d)=((u+v)/2,(u−v)/2), d′=2t d, but its quantitative Theorem 3.2 requires ψ≤ψ2, which our family violates near zero, and Proposition 3.3 assumes a symmetric ψ. Thus merely being in its classified object class does not imply this exact profile. Saito–Kato–Takahashi (2000) treats complex absolute norms; its abstract gives determination/estimation via convex functions, but full-text comparison was inaccessible (institutional DOI lookup resolved unrelated paper), recorded as a residual priority risk rather than falsely ruled out. The same ψ is below ψ2 near z=1, so neither direction of the norm comparison in the cited Proposition 3.1 applies.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The prior facts provide at most a fixed parameter and a qualitative global criterion. They do not determine the norming pairs, exact value, sharp square-to-hexagon threshold or strict minimum for all t>0. Conversely, the new proof recovers the known regular endpoint as a consistency check, not as an independent new statement. The most plausible broad coverage, Komuro–Saito–Mitani 2010, has now been checked in full: its exact-value theorem has a falsified Euclidean majorization hypothesis, even though its extreme-norm classification contains the present objects. Thus its statements do not imply the claimed continuum C_NJ value. The older complex absolute-norm paper has an unresolved priority comparison because its exact full theorem could not be inspected.

originality.rationale: Known p=2 NJ value at t=1 is credited to Yang–Wang and published generalized fixed-hexagon work. The asserted new result is the all-t three-facet deformation exact profile, threshold, strict unique minimum and asymptotic sharpness. Direct comparisons of retrieved primary work, published-finding corpus records and accessible own claims do not imply this continuum formula; see specific checks and named risk below. A six-page full-text comparison with Komuro–Saito–Mitani (2010) identified a precise exclusion from its quantitative theorem, despite its classification of the transformed norms as extreme. The older 2000 complex paper was not available in full and carries explicit residual risk.
residual_risks: Unindexed or differently named computations for the same three-facet hexagon family might predate this work.

The fixed regular-hexagon endpoint is already known and is not assigned novelty.

The full 2000 Saito–Kato–Takahashi complex absolute-norm paper was inaccessible; its results might imply the real family formula under a non-obvious real-complex reduction. Stronger exact coverage has not been established; this is the highest remaining priority risk.

value.rationale: The deformation turns a square into a regular hexagon and then into a thin-strip hexagon via a single natural facet strength. The classical C_NJ constant detects uniform non-squareness. Its complete sharp profile yields a precise activation threshold at t=1/2, the unique optimally non-square member at t=1, a cusp and an exact limiting rate as t tends to infinity; these quantify the geometry of norm deformation beyond a fixed table value.
